title: Celsus should at least have doubted
source_text: Τοσαῦτα δὲ καὶ εἰς τοῦτον εἰπόντες τὸν τόπον ἴδωμεν τοῦ Κέλσου καὶ ἄλλην λέξιν, οὕτως ἔχουσαν· ἐπειδὴ δὲ σώματι συνδεθέντες ἄνθρωποι γεγόνασιν, εἴτ᾿ οἰκονομίας τῶν ὅλων ἕνεκεν εἴτε ποινὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀποτίνοντες, εἴθ᾿ ὑπὸ (πα) θημάτων τινῶν τῆς ψυχῆς βαρυνθείσης, μέχρι ἂν ταῖς τεταγμέναις περιόδοις ἐκκαθαρθῇ· δεῖ γὰρ κατὰ τὸν Ἐμπεδοκλέα τρίς μιν μυρίας ὥρας ἀπὸ μακάρων ἀλάλησθαι, γινομένην παντοίαν διὰ χρόνου ἰδέαν θνητῶν· πειστέον οὖν ὅτι παραδέδονταί τισιν ἐπιμεληταῖς τοῦδε τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου. ὅρα δὴ καὶ ἐν τούτοις περὶ πόσων ἀνθρωπίνως ἀμφιβάλλων καὶ παραθέμενος πλειόνων δόγματα περὶ τῆς αἰτίας τῆς γενέσεως ἡμῶν ἐμφαίνει τινὰ εὐλάβειαν, μὴ τολμῶν ἀποφήνασθαί τι τούτων ψεῦδος εἶναι. ἆρ᾿ οὖν οὐκ ἦν κατὰ τὸν τοιοῦτον, καὶ ἅπαξ κρίναντα μήτε ὡς ἔτυχε συγκαταθέσθαι μήτε τολμηρῶς ἀθετῆσαι τὰ δόξαντα τοῖς ἀρχαίοις. καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰουδαίων λόγου δηλουμένου παρὰ τοῖς ἐκείνων προφήταις καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, εἰ μὴ ἐβούλετο πιστεῦσαι, κἂν ἀμφιβάλλειν καὶ σκοπῆσαι ὅτι εἰκὸς ἦν καὶ τοὺς θεραπεύσαντας τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ ἕνεκεν τῆς εἰς τοῦτον τιμῆς καὶ εἰς τὰ πεπιστευμένα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ νενομοθετῆσθαι πολλάκις μυρίους κινδύνους καὶ θανάτους ἀναδεξαμένους μὴ ὑπερεωρᾶσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοῖς τινα ἐπιφάνειαν γεγονέναι, τὰ μὲν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης περὶ τὰ ἀγάλματα τέχνης ὑπερηφανήσασιν ἀναβαίνειν δὲ πειραθεῖσι τῷ λογισμῷ ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεόν; ἐχρῆν δ᾿ αὐτὸν σκοπῆσαι ὅτι πάντ᾿ ἐφορῶν καὶ πάντ᾿ ἐπακούων ὁ κοινὸς πάντων πατὴρ καὶ δημιουργὸς τὴν ἑκάστου προαίρεσιν, ζητοῦσαν αὐτὸν καὶ εὐσεβεῖν βουλομένην, κατ᾿ ἀξίαν κρίνων καὶ τούτοις τινὰ ἀπονέμει καρπὸν τῆς προστασίας αὐτοῦ, ἵνα μᾶλλον αὔξωσιν ἣν ἅπαξ παρειλήφασι περὶ αὐτοῦ ἔννοιαν. ταῦτα γὰρ εἰ ἐλογίσατο Κέλσος καὶ οἱ μισοῦντες Μωϋσέα καὶ τοὺς ἐν Ἰουδαίοις προφήτας καὶ Ἰησοῦν καὶ τοὺς καμόντας διὰ τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ γνησίους μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ. οὐκ ἂν οὕτως διελοιδορήσαντο Μωϋσεῖ καὶ τοῖς προφήταις καὶ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τοῖς ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ· οὐδὲ μόνους παρὰ πάντα τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς ἔθνη Ἰουδαίους ἀπεδοκίμαζον, λέγοντες αὐτοὺς εἶναι καὶ Αἰγυπτίων χείρονας, τῶν μέχρι ἀλόγων ζῴων εἴτε κατὰ δεισιδαιμονίαν εἴτε κατὰ οἱανδήποτ᾿ αἰτίαν ἢ πλάνην καταγαγόντων τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς τὴν πρὸς τὸ θεῖον τιμήν. ταῦτα δ᾿ εἰρήκαμεν οὐκ ἐπὶ τὸ ἀμφιβάλλειν προτρεπόμενοί τινας περὶ τοῦ κατὰ χριστιανισμὸν λόγου ἀλλὰ παριστάντες ὅτι τοῖς πάντῃ διαλοιδορουμένοις τῷ Χριστιανῶν λόγῳ αἱρετώτερόν ἐστι κἂν ἀμφιβάλλειν περὶ αὐτῶν καὶ μὴ οὕτω θρασέως λέγειν περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἢ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, ἃ μὴ ἐπίστανται καὶ ἀποφαίνονται οὐ μετὰ τῆς καλουμένης παρὰ τοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς „καταληπτικῆς φαντασίας“ οὐδ᾿ ἀπ᾿ ἄλλου τινὸς κριτηρίου, περὶ οὗ ἑκάστη τῶν φιλοσόφων αἵρεσις τὸ φαινόμενον, ὡς ἔδοξε, κατεσκεύασεν.
pass_a_gloss: Having said so much (τοσαῦτα) on this passage (τόπος), let us see another statement (λέξις) of Celsus: since, bound together (συνδέω) to a body (σῶμα), men have come into being (γίγνομαι), whether for the sake of the ordering (οἰκονομία) of the wholes (τὰ ὅλα), or paying (ἀποτίνω) penalties (ποινή) of sin (ἁμαρτία), or the soul weighed down (βαρύνω) by certain passions (πάθημα, editorial supplement), until it be cleansed out (ἐκκαθαίρω) in the appointed (τάσσω) periods (περίοδος); for according to Empedocles it must wander (ἀλάομαι) thrice ten thousand seasons (ὥρα) away from the blessed (μάκαρες), becoming through time every form (ἰδέα) of mortals (θνητός); one must be persuaded (πειστέον) that they have been handed over (παραδίδωμι) to certain overseers (ἐπιμελητής) of this prison (δεσμωτήριον). See how in these too, doubting (ἀμφιβάλλω) humanly (ἀνθρωπίνως) about how many things, and setting beside (παρατίθημι) doctrines (δόγμα) of several about the cause (αἰτία) of our genesis (γένεσις), he displays a certain caution (εὐλάβεια), not daring (τολμάω) to declare (ἀποφαίνομαι) any of these false. Was it not then in keeping with such a man, having once judged (κρίνω) neither to assent (συγκατατίθεμαι) at random (ὡς ἔτυχε) nor boldly (τολμηρῶς) to set aside (ἀθετέω) the things that seemed good to the ancients (ἀρχαῖοι), also concerning the doctrine (λόγος) of the Jews shown in their prophets and concerning Jesus, if he did not wish to believe (πιστεύω), at least (κἄν) to doubt, and to consider (σκοπέω) that it was likely (εἰκός) that those who served (θεραπεύω) the God of all, and for the honour (τιμή) toward him and toward the things believed to have been legislated (νομοθετέω) by him often having undertaken (ἀναδέχομαι) countless dangers (κίνδυνος) and deaths, were not overlooked (ὑπεροράω) by God, but that some manifestation (ἐπιφάνεια) came about for them too, having disdained (ὑπερηφανέω) the things of human art (τέχνη) about statues (ἄγαλμα) and having tried (πειράομαι) to ascend (ἀναβαίνω) by reasoning (λογισμός) to the God over all himself? He ought to have considered that, overseeing all (ἐφοράω) and hearing all (ἐπακούω), the common Father (πατήρ) and Creator (δημιουργός) of all, judging according to worth (κατ᾿ ἀξίαν) the choice (προαίρεσις) of each, seeking him and wishing to be pious (εὐσεβέω), assigns (ἀπονέμω) to these too some fruit (καρπός) of his protection (προστασία), that they may increase (αὐξάνω) more the conception (ἔννοια) about him which they once received (παραλαμβάνω). For if Celsus had reckoned (λογίζομαι) these things, and those hating Moses and the prophets among the Jews and Jesus and his genuine (γνήσιος) disciples who toiled/wore themselves out (κάμνω) for his word, they would not so have reviled (διαλοιδορέομαι) Moses and the prophets and Jesus and his apostles; nor would they have rejected (ἀποδοκιμάζω) the Jews alone beside all nations (ἔθνη) on earth, saying they are worse (χείρων) even than the Egyptians, who as far as in them brought down (κατάγω) the honour toward the divine (τὸ θεῖον) even to irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα), whether by superstition (δεισιδαιμονία) or by whatever cause or error (πλάνη). We have said these things not urging (προτρέπω) some to doubt about the doctrine according to Christianity (χριστιανισμός), but showing (παρίστημι) that for those reviling in every way the doctrine of Christians it is more choiceworthy (αἱρετώτερον) at least to doubt about them and not to speak so rashly (θρασέως) about Jesus or his disciples things they do not know (ἐπίσταμαι), and declare not with what is called among those from the Stoa (Στοά) cognitive impression (καταληπτικὴ φαντασία), nor from any other criterion (κριτήριον), about which each school (αἵρεσις) of philosophers constructed (κατασκευάζω) what appeared (τὸ φαινόμενον), as seemed good.
pass_b_english: Having said this much on this passage as well, let us look at another statement of Celsus, which runs thus: “Since men are born bound to a body — whether for the sake of the ordering of the universe, or paying the penalty for sin, or because the soul is weighed down by certain passions until it is cleansed in the appointed cycles, for according to Empedocles ‘thrice ten thousand seasons it must wander far from the blessed, becoming in the course of time every kind of mortal form’ (Empedocles, fragment 115) — we must therefore believe that they have been handed over to certain keepers of this prison.”

See how here too he wavers, as a man will, over so many questions, and by setting out the opinions of several thinkers on the cause of our coming into being he shows a certain caution, not daring to declare any one of them false. Would it not, then, have befitted such a man, once he had resolved neither to assent at random nor boldly to set aside the views of the ancients, at least to doubt, if he did not wish to believe, about the teaching of the Jews set forth in their prophets and about Jesus? Would it not have befitted him to consider that it was likely that those who served the God of all, and who for the sake of honour toward him and toward what they believed he had laid down as law often accepted countless dangers and deaths, were not overlooked by God, but that some manifestation came to them also, since they had disdained the works of human art in statues and tried to ascend by reason to the God over all himself?

He ought to have considered that the common Father and Creator of all, who sees all things and hears all things, judges according to its worth the choice of each person that seeks him and wishes to be devout, and grants to these also some fruit of his protection, so that they may further increase the conception of him which they have once received. For if Celsus had reasoned this out, and with him those who hate Moses and the prophets among the Jews, and Jesus, and his genuine disciples who wore themselves out for the sake of his word, they would not have heaped such abuse on Moses and the prophets and Jesus and his apostles. Nor would they have rejected the Jews alone of all the nations on earth, saying that they were worse even than the Egyptians, who, as far as lay in them, brought the honour paid to the divine down even to irrational animals, whether from superstition or for whatever other cause or error.

We have said this not to urge anyone to doubt about the Christian teaching, but to show that for those who revile the teaching of Christians in every way it would be better at least to doubt about these matters, and not to speak so rashly about Jesus or his disciples. For they speak of things they do not know, and they make their declarations without what the Stoics call the cognitive impression and without any other criterion; and on the criterion each school of philosophers has argued for its own view, as it thought best.

choices.choice: Celsus’s quotation runs from ‘Since men are born’ to ‘this prison’; the Empedocles line sits inside it in single quotes, and the dashes mark off Celsus’s list of possible causes so that ‘we must therefore believe’ reads as his main clause. Empedocles, fragment 115 Diels-Kranz, lines 6-7: the received Empedocles text has φυόμενον παντοῖα ... εἴδεα; Celsus’s version reads γινομένην παντοίαν ... ἰδέαν, rendered as it stands here. πα(θημάτων) is an editorial supplement in the staged text; translated as ‘passions’. ἀνθρωπίνως ἀμφιβάλλων is rendered ‘wavers, as a man will’. ‘Who sees all things and hears all things’ (πάντ᾿ ἐφορῶν καὶ πάντ᾿ ἐπακούων) borrows the Homeric formula used of the Sun (Homer, Iliad 3.277) and applies it to God; left without an inline citation because Origen is not quoting Homer for his sense. τοὺς καμόντας (‘who wore themselves out’) can also carry the Homeric sense ‘the dead’; ‘wore themselves out for the sake of his word’ keeps both effort and suffering without adding martyrdom outright. The Greek’s single long question in the second paragraph is split, and the frame ‘Would it not have befitted him’ is repeated before ‘to consider’; no content added. τολμηρῶς is ‘boldly’ and θρασέως ‘rashly’, keeping the two words apart. ‘Cognitive impression’ renders the Stoic technical term καταληπτικὴ φαντασία. The last clause (περὶ οὗ ... κατεσκεύασεν) is rendered ‘and on the criterion each school of philosophers has argued for its own view, as it thought best’; ‘on the criterion’ makes the antecedent of οὗ explicit. Celsus’s claim that the Jews are worse than the Egyptians is not quoted here; no reference supplied.
Celsus's quotation: dashes mark off the list of causes so 'we must therefore believe' reads as the main clause (was a run-on 'for ..., we must therefore')
Split question: sentence fragment 'And to consider ...' -> 'Would it not have befitted him to consider ...'
'honour due to the divine' -> 'honour paid to the divine' (τὴν πρὸς τὸ θεῖον τιμήν; 'due' was an addition)
θρασέως 'boldly' -> 'rashly' (keeps it apart from τολμηρῶς 'boldly' above)
Last clause: concessive 'though' (not in the Greek) -> relative sense 'and on the criterion each school ...'; quotation marks removed from the Stoic term so they are not mistaken for Celsus's words

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
